props.title: Fast, Cheap & Out of Control

sections.content: Errol Morris's Fast, Cheap & Out of Control is a masterwork of documentary interconnection, weaving together four seemingly unrelated subjects: a topiary gardener, a naked mole rat researcher, a lion tamer, and a roboticist. Through Morris's signature Interrotron interview style and Caleb Sampson's haunting circus-like score, the film creates surprising parallels between man's attempts to shape and control nature. Like Morris's earlier The Thin Blue Line (1988), it uses stylized recreations and dynamic cinematography by Robert Richardson to elevate documentary beyond simple observation.

sections.content: The film represents a crucial evolution in Morris's style, building on techniques he developed in A Brief History of Time (1991) but pushing further into experimental territory. The rapid cutting between subjects and blend of 16mm, 35mm, and video formats creates a hypnotic effect that mirrors the obsessive nature of his subjects. This approach influenced later hybrid documentaries like Stories We Tell (2012) and The Act of Killing (2012), which similarly blur the lines between documentation and artistic interpretation.

Morris's use of the Interrotron, his patented interview device that allows subjects to make direct eye contact with the camera while seeing Morris's face, achieves an unprecedented intimacy with his subjects. This technique would later influence documentarians like Werner Herzog in films like Grizzly Man (2005) and Into the Abyss (2011), where direct address creates powerful emotional connections with interview subjects. sections.content: The film's innovative structure anticipates the fragmented, associative style that would become more common in contemporary documentaries like I'm Still Here (2010) and The Missing Picture (2013). Morris breaks from traditional documentary's emphasis on clear narrative progression, instead creating a meditation on human nature through pattern and metaphor. His subjects' seemingly disparate obsessions - from sculpting hedges to studying naked mole rats - become a lens for examining humanity's desire to impose order on chaos.
